title: Prayer That Connects
subtitle: A pattern that was given on purpose, because people asked how.
objectives: Explain why the disciples asked to be taught to pray
Name the parts of the Lord's Prayer pattern
Use the ACTS structure for prayer
Explain Philippians 4:6-7 in your own words
Explain what praying continually means in practice

cards.title: They asked how, not whether
cards.text: In Luke 11 the disciples ask to be taught to pray. Nobody asks that unless it is a skill, and they were treating it as one.

cards.title: He gave them a shape, not a script
cards.text: "This, then, is how you should pray." It is short, and every line does a different job.
points: **Who God is** — before anything is asked for.
**Today's needs** — daily bread, not a year's.

cards.title: Four parts, in order
cards.text: A common way to remember the same shape. Tap through each one.

question.text: Why did the disciples ask to be taught to pray?
options: They were treating prayer as a skill that could be learned
They had never heard of prayer
question.explain: Nobody asks to be taught something unless it is learnable. The answer given is a pattern, not a script.

cards.title: Asking comes last, and that is deliberate
cards.text: Most people start with what they want. The pattern puts three things before it, and none of them is a delay tactic.

cards.title: Nobody skips straight to the hard rounds
cards.text: Every session has an order, and the order is not decoration. Skipping to the part you want makes that part worse.
points: **A pattern removes the decision** each session.
**You do not renegotiate it** when tired.
**Same reason** the prayer has a shape.

question.text: Put the ACTS pattern in order.
question.explain: Who God is, then honesty, then thanks, then asking. Asking comes last on purpose.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Part 2 is what prayer is for, and what praying continually actually means. Your place is saved.

cards.title: It is called connecting for a reason
cards.text: The word in the title is not decoration. Every passage about prayer treats it as a relationship rather than a request form.

cards.title: Do not be anxious. Ask instead
cards.text: In everything, by prayer and thanksgiving, present your requests. The promise that follows is peace, not always the thing asked for.
points: **The promise is peace**, which is worth noticing.
**It does not promise the outcome you asked for.**

cards.title: Scale is part of the point
cards.text: Psalm 19 opens with the heavens declaring the glory of God. Looking up is a very old way of putting a problem in proportion.
points: **A problem does not shrink**, but you see it differently.

question.text: What does Philippians 4:6-7 promise will follow prayer?
question.explain: Peace, described as guarding your heart and mind. The passage does not promise the outcome you requested.

cards.title: What "pray continually" actually means
cards.text: It cannot mean speaking non-stop, because nobody could. It means keeping the line open rather than only opening it in emergencies.
points: **Short and often** beats long and rare.
**On the walk, before the test, after training.**
**"Give thanks in all circumstances"** is the same passage.

cards.title: Frequency beats duration in almost everything
cards.text: Ten minutes daily builds more than seventy minutes on a Sunday. That is true of language, of training, and of this.
points: **Little and often** is how habits set.
**A long gap** is what breaks a routine.

question.text: "Pray continually" means you should be speaking prayers non-stop all day.
question.explain: False. Nobody could. It describes keeping the line open rather than only opening it in emergencies.

terms.def: The pattern given in Matthew 6:9-13. A shape to follow, not a script to recite.
Saying who God is, before asking for anything.
Being honest about what you got wrong.
Asking, for yourself and for others. It comes last in the pattern.
Do not be anxious; pray with thanksgiving. The promise that follows is peace.
Pray continually. Short and often rather than long and rare.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **They asked to be taught.** It is a skill.
**Continually means short and often**, not non-stop.

quiz.text: What did the disciples ask Jesus in Luke 11?
options: Whether they should pray at all
quiz.explain: They treated prayer as a skill to be learned, and the answer they got was a pattern.
quiz.objective: Explain why the disciples asked to be taught to pray

quiz.text: Where is the Lord's Prayer found?
quiz.explain: Matthew 6:9-13, introduced with 'this, then, is how you should pray'.
quiz.objective: Name the parts of the Lord's Prayer pattern

quiz.text: What comes FIRST in the ACTS pattern?
quiz.explain: Adoration — saying who God is, before anything is asked for.
quiz.objective: Use the ACTS structure for prayer

quiz.text: Put the ACTS pattern in the right order.
quiz.explain: Adoration, confession, thanksgiving, supplication. Asking is last, and that is deliberate.
quiz.objective: Use the ACTS structure for prayer

options: Asking, for yourself and for other people
Listing what you are thankful for
quiz.explain: Asking. It comes last in the pattern, which is not the same as mattering least.
quiz.objective: Use the ACTS structure for prayer

quiz.text: In the Lord's Prayer, what is asked for in terms of food?
quiz.explain: Daily bread. Today's needs, not next year's, which is part of the shape of the prayer.
quiz.objective: Name the parts of the Lord's Prayer pattern

quiz.text: What does Philippians 4:6-7 promise will follow prayer?
options: Peace that guards your heart and mind
quiz.explain: Peace. The passage is careful, and it does not promise the outcome you requested.
quiz.objective: Explain Philippians 4:6-7 in your own words

quiz.text: What does Philippians 4:6 say should go with your requests?
quiz.explain: With thanksgiving. It is part of the instruction, not an optional extra.
quiz.objective: Explain Philippians 4:6-7 in your own words

quiz.text: Philippians 4:6-7 promises that you will get whatever you ask for.
quiz.explain: False. What is promised is peace guarding your heart and mind, which is a different promise.
quiz.objective: Explain Philippians 4:6-7 in your own words

quiz.text: What does "pray continually" mean in practice?
options: Short and often, keeping the line open
Praying for at least an hour daily
quiz.explain: Nobody could speak non-stop. It describes frequency, not duration. 1 Thessalonians 5:17.
quiz.objective: Explain what praying continually means in practice

quiz.text: Which passage says "give thanks in all circumstances"?
quiz.explain: The same short passage that says pray continually. The three instructions sit together.
quiz.objective: Explain what praying continually means in practice

quiz.text: The Lord's Prayer was given as a pattern to follow rather than only as words to recite.
quiz.explain: True. 'This, then, is how you should pray.' Every line in it does a different job.
quiz.objective: Name the parts of the Lord's Prayer pattern

teacher.summary: Week 5 Devotion covers prayer, matching the Term 1 theme and completing the subject. It opens on a detail that reframes the topic: the disciples asked to be taught, which means they were treating prayer as a learnable skill, and the answer they were given was a shape rather than a script. ACTS is used as the memorable form of that shape, with the ordering explained rather than asserted — asking comes last, and the three things before it are not delays. Philippians 4:6-7 is handled precisely, because the promise in it is peace rather than the requested outcome, and reading it as a guarantee of results sets a student up for disappointment. 'Pray continually' is explained as frequency rather than duration, which is both the honest reading and the practical one.
discussion: Ask him why the disciples asked to be taught. Treating it as a skill is a more useful starting point than treating it as a mood.
Ask what changes if you put thanksgiving before asking. He can test that in one sitting.
Ask what Philippians 4 actually promises. Noticing that it says peace rather than results is the most important thing in the lesson.
Ask what 'continually' can possibly mean if nobody can speak non-stop.
teacher.extension: Have him try the four-part shape once a day for a week, keeping each part to a sentence. Four sentences is short enough to actually repeat, which is the whole argument of the second half.
misconceptions: 'The Lord's Prayer is only words to recite.' It is introduced as a pattern: this is how you should pray.
'Philippians 4 promises you get what you ask for.' What it promises is peace guarding your heart and mind.
'Pray continually means non-stop talking.' Nobody could. It is about frequency, not duration.
'Asking comes last because it matters least.' It comes last because the three parts before it change how you ask.
